label: Kendall Similarity Shape Spaces
notes: This short chapter, printed pages 82 through 86, builds Kendall's shape space step by step. A configuration of landmarks becomes a shape only after we quotient away translation, scale, and rotation. The whole pipeline is the foundation for every later inference statement on shapes.

label: Landmarks and Configurations
notes: We start with k labelled landmarks in m dimensions, stacked as a configuration matrix. Two configurations should be called the same shape when they differ only by a similarity transformation. This slide fixes notation and motivates why raw coordinates are the wrong thing to compare directly.

label: Removing Translation
notes: Translation is removed by centering each configuration at its centroid, equivalently multiplying by the Helmert submatrix. The result lives in an m by k minus one dimensional subspace where the column sums vanish. This is the first quotient and it discards exactly m degrees of freedom.

label: Removing Scale: The Pre-shape Sphere
notes: After centering we divide by the Frobenius norm, the centroid size, fixing unit size. Centered unit-size configurations form the pre-shape sphere, a sphere of dimension m times k minus one, minus one. Pre-shapes still carry an arbitrary rotation, so they are not yet shapes.

label: Rotation Orbits
notes: The rotation group SO(m) acts on the pre-shape sphere, sweeping each pre-shape around an orbit. All pre-shapes in one orbit represent the same physical shape. The shape is the orbit itself, so the shape space is the set of these rotation orbits on the sphere.

label: The Quotient Shape Space
notes: Kendall's shape space is the pre-shape sphere quotiented by SO(m). Its dimension is the sphere dimension minus the dimension of the rotation group. We collapse each orbit to a single point, and that quotient point is the similarity shape of the landmark configuration.

label: Dimension Count
notes: Counting carefully: mk coordinates, minus m for translation, minus one for scale, minus the rotation group dimension m choose two. For planar shapes this gives two k minus two, the complex projective space familiar from Kendall's original construction of planar shapes.

label: Riemannian Submersion
notes: The quotient map is a Riemannian submersion. Tangent vectors split into vertical directions, tangent to the orbit, and horizontal directions, orthogonal to it. Only horizontal motion changes the shape, so the shape metric is read off from horizontal vectors on the pre-shape sphere.

label: Procrustes Registration
notes: To compare two pre-shapes we optimally rotate one onto the other, the Procrustes registration solved by the singular value decomposition of their cross-product. The optimal rotation aligns them as closely as possible, and the residual angle after alignment is what the shape distance measures.

label: Procrustes and Geodesic Distance
notes: The shape distance is the geodesic distance on the quotient, equal to the arc-cosine of the maximal alignment correlation. It equals the great-circle angle between orbits, achieved at the Procrustes-optimal rotation. This invariant distance underlies every Frechet mean and test built later in the course.

label: Singularities and Degeneracy
notes: Orbits have constant dimension only where the configuration is non-degenerate. Collinear or otherwise rank-deficient configurations have smaller stabilizers shrinking their orbits, creating singular strata. Away from these singularities the shape space is a smooth manifold, which is where nonparametric inference is well behaved.

label: Recap and Outlook
notes: We assembled the shape space as a tower of quotients: center, scale, then rotate away. The pre-shape sphere and its rotation orbits give a Riemannian submersion whose Procrustes geodesic distance is the working metric. Next chapters put means and tests on this curved stage.
